criterion_notes.c1: Examines urban drinking-water service delivery and household/user access across two municipal water utilities in Saltillo and Hermosillo, Mexico (covering 228,245 and 259,168 domestic connections respectively), including drinking-water coverage, 24/7 service continuity vs. rationing, new connection subsidies, and service disconnections.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Plain reading: evaluates institutional capacity, governance autonomy, and administrative management of two municipal water utilities. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: directly examines (1) utility ownership and regulatory governance structure (mixed public-private company Aguas de Saltillo under a 25-year association/technical-assistance contract vs. decentralized municipal public utility Agua de Hermosillo); (2) tariff and cost-recovery rules (mandatory monthly inflation-indexed tariffs vs. non-indexed state congress approval, social/preferential tariffs 'tarifa social' and 'tarifa popular', cross-subsidized connection fee reductions for low-income households, and discretionary flat-rate billing on unmetered connections); and (3) statutory enforcement vs. clientelist discretion/accommodation in non-payment disconnections (limitation at 2 months and disconnection at 3 months with health/social-assistance exemptions in Saltillo vs. discretionary non-enforcement and fee waivers via Unión de Usuarios in Hermosillo).
criterion_notes.c3: Empirical comparative longitudinal case study (2001–2015) drawing on utility legal/contractual documents, key informant interviews, longitudinal utility indicators from Conagua, PIGOO/IMTA, and annual utility reports, plus INEGI national household survey data (ENCIG, ENSU).
criterion_notes.c4: Reports drinking-water coverage (98% in Hermosillo vs. 99% in Saltillo), 24/7 service continuity and rationing (continuity rising from 10% in 2001 to 74% in 2015 in Saltillo; 24/7 supply with periodic 8-hour/day rationing in Hermosillo), user-reported supply failures/leaks and service satisfaction, and qualitative evidence on non-payment disconnections and exemptions/waivers, alongside utility physical/commercial efficiency and operating balance.
criterion_notes.c5: Unit of analysis is the municipal water utility (N = 2 utilities: Aguas de Saltillo and Agua de Hermosillo, serving 243,696 and 275,062 total connections including 228,245 and 259,168 domestic connections in Saltillo, Coahuila, and Hermosillo, Sonora, 2001–2015). Exposure, access/continuity outcomes, and comparative case-study design are clearly specified. Note that N=2 utility-level comparison will contribute primarily to the narrative/mechanism synthesis rather than quantitative meta-analysis (Criterion 6 is a synthesis gate, not a review-eligibility gate).
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in Spanish (with English and Spanish abstracts). Per Inclusion Criterion 10, non-English/Portuguese/Dutch studies are eligible when translation from the accessible full text is feasible and the study is mechanism-relevant; Spanish full text was directly assessed and translation method should be logged in extraction_note.

evidence_quotes.quote: En 2001, Saltillo transitó de una administración paramunicipal hacia un esquema de empresa mixta público-privada (Aguas de Saltillo), mientras que el organismo de agua potable de la ciudad de Hermosillo dejó de ser un organismo bajo la administración estatal y en el año 2002 se convirtió en la paramunicipal Agua de Hermosillo.

En el año 2012 el presidente municipal, Jericó Abramo Masso, negoció una reducción en el cobro de las conexiones nuevas para usuarios de bajos ingresos, a cambio de un incremento en las tarifas para financiar el subsidio a la conexión.

Ambos organismos cuentan con tarifas preferenciales para apoyar a las personas de escasos recursos. En el caso de Hermosillo, cuenta con la denominada “tarifa social”, mientras que Saltillo cuenta con la “tarifa popular”. En Hermosillo el manejo discrecional de tarifas ha permitido el uso político de las mismas.

En Saltillo, la Ley de Aguas para los Municipios de Coahuila establece que en caso de mora en el pago de dos meses, se limitará el suministro, y a los tres meses se suspenderá totalmente. Los únicos casos en que no se llevará a cabo el corte del servicio es cuando se trate de edificios de servicios asistenciales, o por razones de salud y/o de seguridad pública.

En Hermosillo, la ley de aguas faculta al organismo para suspender el servicio en caso de falta de pago: se puede cortar el servicio de los usuarios que tengan adeudos de más de dos meses. Sin embargo, la suspensión de servicios se aplica de manera discrecional, pues los afiliados a la organización denominada “Unión de Usuarios” pueden evitar el corte, aun cuando no paguen por el servicio debido a la presión política ejercida por la organización.

La información para este análisis se basó en la revisión de documentos de ambos OOA; entrevistas a informantes clave, estadísticas de la Comisión Nacional del Agua (Conagua), del Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Geografía (INEGI) y del Programa de Indicadores de Organismos Operadores (PIGOO) del Instituto Mexicano de Tecnología del Agua (IMTA).

La cobertura de servicios de agua potable es alta en ambas ciudades (98% en Hermosillo y 99% en Saltillo). En Hermosillo, el suministro es de 24 horas continuas, los 7 días de la semana. En algunos años se ha aplicado el racionamiento, reduciendo el suministro a 8 horas diarias. En Saltillo, en 2001 solo 10 por ciento de los usuarios contaba con servicio continuo los 7 días de la semana, mientras que para 2015 este indicador subió a 74 por ciento (Aguas de Saltillo, 2016).

raw_response.exposure: Utility ownership and governance/regulatory rules: mixed public-private utility ownership (Aguas de Saltillo, 51% municipal / 49% private operator) vs. decentralized municipal public utility (Agua de Hermosillo), including mandatory monthly inflation-indexed tariffs vs. politicized non-indexed tariff setting, social/preferential tariffs and low-income connection fee cross-subsidies, universal metering vs. discretionary unmetered flat-rate billing, and rule-bound statutory enforcement vs. clientelistic discretion in non-payment disconnections.
raw_response.outcome: Drinking-water service coverage (98% vs. 99%), 24/7 service continuity and rationing (rising from 10% to 74% continuous supply in Saltillo; 24/7 supply with periodic 8-hour daily rationing in Hermosillo), user-reported supply failures/leaks and service satisfaction, disconnection enforcement/waivers, and utility physical/commercial efficiency and operating balance.
raw_response.population_and_sample: Unit of analysis: municipal water utilities (N = 2 utilities: Aguas de Saltillo in Saltillo, Coahuila, serving 243,696 connections including 228,245 domestic connections in a municipality of 807,537 residents; and Agua de Hermosillo in Hermosillo, Sonora, serving 275,062 connections including 259,168 domestic connections in a municipality of 884,273 residents), evaluated over 2001–2015.
raw_response.rationale: This empirical comparative case study evaluates two Mexican municipal drinking-water utilities (2001–2015) using key informant interviews, legal/contractual review, and longitudinal administrative and household-survey indicators. It satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2 because it directly analyzes utility ownership structure (mixed public-private company vs. paramunicipal utility), tariff and cost-recovery rules (inflation indexation, preferential social tariffs, connection-fee cross-subsidies for low-income households, and unmetered flat-rate discretion), and statutory vs. discretionary/clientelist enforcement of non-payment service disconnections alongside drinking-water coverage, 24/7 service continuity, rationing, and user-reported supply failures. Full text is in Spanish and directly translatable per Criterion 10.
raw_response.study_design: Comparative longitudinal mixed-methods case study (documentary/legal review, key informant interviews, and 2001–2015 utility administrative and survey indicators)
